prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are interrogated in large numbers, bringing frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B012 with Katori and Ye as a single prize part. Nothing in the round-1 exchange weakened the scientific core: the magic-wavelength lattice cancels the light shift for a narrow transition while thousands of neutral atoms are interrogated at once, it has been reproduced in several independent laboratories, and it has produced results that reach beyond metrology, namely 10^-18 uncertainty, relativistic geodesy and tighter limits on varying constants. The chair asks whether the overlap with 2005 and 2012 can be settled in the wording rather than in the names, and I think it can. A citation that names the lattice and many-atom interrogation recognises the idea that is new, and it treats combs and single-ion control as tools the lattice clock uses, not as achievements being awarded again. The two-name allocation is the cleanest on the shortlist. I did not change my preferred configuration from round 1. What changed is that I now treat the citation as part of the scientific judgment, and I would insist that it not rest on accuracy in general, since ion clocks reach comparable uncertainty.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining objection is credit. Takamoto, Hong, Ludlow, Lemke and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups, and the Sr versus Yb first-demonstration history, are not covered by two names, and none of us has been able to verify that history from the materials we are allowed to use. If the first-demonstration record turned out to favour a different pairing, the configuration would have to be reopened, and I would rather say that now than assume the citation can repair any omission. A second objection is the lineage argument: after 2005 and 2012, a sceptic can still read this as an evolutionary refinement of precision metrology. I think the many-atom lattice answers that, but Eriksson is entitled to judge otherwise. I also accept that Pearce is right that B042 has the larger recent footprint, and that a conceptually new field could in principle outrank an instrument achievement.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B030 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as the sole part, holds that a conceptual advance should outrank a precision-measurement advance, and ranked B012 eighth, treating the pending redefinition of the second as leaving the impact unfinished.
responses.response: I agree that B030 is mature and that his case for the HgTe observation is real. I still disagree on the ordering for two reasons. First, the distinction between concept and instrument does not fit this candidate: the magic-wavelength lattice is a concept, a state-independent trap for a clock transition, and the instrument followed from it. Second, the redefinition of the second is a metrological decision that depends on several clock families and on comparison campaigns. The scientific achievement, 10^-18 reproduced in independent laboratories, exists without it. Against B030, the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is a more serious credit gap than anything in B012, and the 2016 prize on topological phases that he raises himself weakens its novelty. I would retain B030 as my first alternative and would ask whether he can accept B012 as lead with B030 kept for a later year.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that state-independent trapping is an original atomic-structure insight that builds on combs and single-ion control without duplicating them, and that the citation should be careful about who demonstrated what first.
responses.response: I agree and I take her point as the best answer to the overlap objection, since she is the member best placed to judge the atomic structure. Her own caution about first-demonstration credit I share fully. My additional demand is on wording: the citation should say lattice and many-atom interrogation and should not say accuracy in general, because ion clocks reach comparable accuracy and that is the territory the 2012 prize already covered. I also agree with her that a second part would not be fair: with a three-person cap it could carry only one name from B030 or B042, and that split would be arbitrary.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, now concedes that the B042 attribution is less settled than he assumed, but notes that B042 has the larger recent footprint and that a new field could deserve priority over a very mature precision-measurement achievement.
responses.response: I value that he states the concession openly, and I share his reading of the footprint. Our difference is maturity and not merit. About eight years after the experiments the origin of the superconductivity and of several correlated states is unsettled, the experimental credit divides across Jarillo-Herrero, Cao, Dean, Young, Efetov and others, and Bistritzer's inclusion is doubted by Olsson. A prize that has to name three people today would settle these questions by drawing a line that the field has not yet drawn. If the mechanism and the credit were clearer I could support B042 in a later year, and that is why it remains my second alternative. In answer to the chair's question on B042, I would not support it as lead now.

responses.point: Kroll supports B012 first, argues that the redefinition of the second should not be a precondition, and notes that the 2012 prizes did not block the 2025 award, so the overlap risk is symmetric.
responses.response: I agree that the redefinition should not be a precondition, and I would put the argument more strongly: tying a prize to a metrological body's timetable would give an external process a vote on our scientific judgment. I accept the symmetric-risk point on timing, but it works differently for B012 than for B005. The 2025 prize concerned macroscopic tunnelling in superconducting circuits, and circuit QED would follow it from the same line of work within a year, which is the reason I do not put B005 forward. On his B020 ranking, I would not push it as a preferred part, since it carries the overlap with Wineland and sits close to my own WACQT conflict.

responses.point: Olsson says that early lattice-clock credit cannot be fixed by adding a third name that is not on the shortlist, and that the novelty and credit questions should be answered in the citation text.
responses.response: I agree that we cannot add a name that is not on the shortlist, and that a third name from the shortlist is not available here either. This means the only honest remedy is citation wording that is narrow and accurate about what Katori and Ye are credited with: the concept and first strontium lattice clock for Katori, and the record accuracy, coherence and applications at JILA for Ye. I would go one step further than her and say that if the committee cannot confirm the first-demonstration history, the citation should avoid the word 'first'.

uncertainties: Whether the first-demonstration and credit history of Sr and Yb lattice clocks (Takamoto, Hong, Ludlow, Lemke, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) is consistent with a Katori and Ye pairing; I cannot verify it from the materials I am allowed to use.
Whether Eriksson accepts citation wording around the magic-wavelength lattice as resolving his novelty concern about the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Whether B042 will be resolvable, on mechanism and attribution, in a later year.
Whether my closeness to superconducting quantum technology makes me unconsciously discount candidates (B005, B020) that the committee might otherwise weigh more heavily.
statement.conflict_note: My disclosure is unchanged. I direct WACQT at Chalmers, work in circuit and waveguide QED, and have documented links to Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson and to frequent co-author Anton Frisk Kockum. This is a possible conflict for B005 and for other superconducting-circuit and quantum-computing candidates such as B020 and B002, so I do not propose them as preferred or alternative. For B012, B030 and B042 no specific conflict follows from my profile, and I do not claim any confidential committee knowledge.
